rationale: Group the three arms by the state of the protein they leave behind. Deleting the gene leaves no PRMT7. The degrader leaves almost none either: it ties PRMT7 to VHL for proteasomal destruction without touching its transcript, and in T cells the treated cells look like deleted cells - less PRMT7, more p65 in the nucleus. Sharing a warhead with the inhibitor is irrelevant; what the molecule does to protein levels is what counts. The inhibitor is the odd one out: PRMT7 stays, only its catalytic site is occupied, and we know occupancy happens in cells because pre-dosing with it stops the degrader from working, which rules out the lazy explanation that the compound never engaged. Now ask whether catalysis is the part that matters. A point mutant with no enzymatic activity still associates with p65 and still shuts down the p65 reporter to the same degree as the wild-type enzyme, so what restrains p65 is the presence of the protein. Occupying the active site thus leaves the restraint running, while deletion or degradation lifts it. Lifting it favours CD8+ cells rather than harming them: PRMT7-null T cells show nuclear p65, higher Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, CD25 and ICAM, and fewer apoptosis transcripts, and the CD8+ gap vanishes when NF-kB is blocked with BAY 11-7082. Both protein-removal arms should therefore show more CD8+ cells, not fewer. The fall to roughly 11% belongs to SGC3027.
